extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and attorneys subject to USPTO disciplinary rules; OED attorneys, tribunal members, and counsel handling USPTO discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria the USPTO Tribunal uses to evaluate alleged attorney misconduct (e.g., false statements, failure to pay judgments/taxes, discovery noncompliance, altered evidence) and the evidentiary/authentication practices relevant to those determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility prohibited practitioners from engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct. Disreputable conduct has generally included unprofessional conduct and any conduct violative of the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in decision: failure to timely file and pay federal and state income taxes; failure to pay court-ordered judgments. Tribunal may look to prior USPTO disciplinary decisions (e.g., In re Miller, In re Halvonik) for application. The USPTO regulations declined to further define the terms, but tribunals treat them as including conduct evincing lack of professional obligation, probity, or honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal conduct adversely reflecting on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a lawyer to commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on the practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a practitioner in other respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere commission of a criminal act does not automatically reflect adversely on fitness; context matters. Willful failure to file income tax returns and pay taxes has been treated as a criminal act reflecting adversely on fitness. 'Willful' is defined as a voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty (United States v. Pomponio). Tribunal needs evidence (or admission) of voluntariness/intent to find a criminal act under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly disobey obligations under rules of a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal except for an 'open refusal' based upon an assertion that no valid obligation exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Open refusal' is defined as good faith and open noncompliance to test an order's validity. Challenging an order by motions/appeals is insufficient to excuse noncompliance absent a stay; practitioners remain obligated to comply. Examples: failing to remit payment on court judgments constitutes knowingly disobeying tribunal obligations where remedies were denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly make false statement of fact or law to a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Knowingly' means with actual knowledge of the fact in question; knowledge may be inferred from circumstances. 'Tribunal' includes USPTO, courts, arbitrators in binding arbitration, administrative agencies, or other adjudicative bodies. Examples: false answers in reinstatement questionnaires, omissions in bankruptcy schedules, and false statements in OED investigations violate this rule; failure to correct prior false statements also violates the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunals may look to common dictionary definitions: 'dishonesty' = lack of truth/honesty/trustworthiness; 'deceit' = quality of being dishonest or misleading; 'misrepresentation' = making a false or misleading assertion (including conduct amounting to a false assertion). Intent to deceive is often required for sanctionable dishonesty/misrepresentation; mere failure to pay pre-rule obligations may not suffice without evidence of intent. False statements and fabricated evidence are examples of conduct violating this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond to a lawful demand or request for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner, in connection with a disciplinary matter, shall not knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information unless disclosure is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Knowingly' requires actual knowledge. Examples of violations include omitting required documents from responses to RFIs, promising to provide documents and never doing so, providing evasive or non-responsive written answers, and giving false or misleading responses. Repeated requests for extensions/tolling and other dilatory tactics can demonstrate intentional non-cooperation. Tribunal may find violations even where answers are partially provided if supporting documentation is withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of altered, fabricated, or manufactured evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting evidence that has been altered, fabricated, or otherwise manufactured is egregious misconduct and undermines the integrity of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal considers whether evidence contains anomalies inconsistent with normal creation/transmission (e.g., formatting/header anomalies, embedded vs. attached invoices). Demonstrated ability to manipulate emails and headers (e.g., using web apps to change format, dates, and header characters) supports finding alteration. Motivation (e.g., to surprise opponent) and withholding exhibits increases sanction severity. Admission of such fabricated evidence supports findings of dishonesty, deceit, and related violations of professional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary/authentication standards for emails and digital forensic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentication of emails and digital files requires defensible forensic collection, preservation of metadata and headers, and use of best practices and multiple data sources where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: experts should personally collect data from original devices, preserve metadata and headers, collect from multiple locations/sources, and avoid relying solely on copies provided by an interested party. Header 'hop' data and origin/path fields can be insufficient or manipulated; demonstrative testing can show header information may be altered by applications. Expert opinions based solely on headers or single-source data are less persuasive. Tribunal gives greater weight to experts who employ defensible collection methods and who can demonstrate preservation and analysis processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting expert testimony on digital evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal assesses expert credibility and weight based on qualifications, methods used, and whether the expert personally collected and defensibly preserved the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts who personally collect data from devices and preserve metadata are given greater weight than those relying only on materials provided by a party. Experts should follow 'best practice' (multiple sources, defensible collection) and be able to explain methodology; failure to do so undermines conclusions. Demonstrations of reproducible manipulations (e.g., altering headers/dates via editing tools) bolster the reliability of contrary expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of objections to exhibits due to prior provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to exhibits previously provided to the Tribunal and the opposing party may be waived if not timely raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exhibits were previously provided and the tribunal ruled objections were waived, late objections (e.g., at the hearing) are untimely and disingenuous. Physical possession of exhibits by the objecting party and prior notice can support a finding of waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtroom decorum and behavior as a factor in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of decorum (e.g., interrupting the tribunal, mischaracterizing testimony, attempting to testify through questioning, insulting witnesses) evidences unprofessional conduct that can inform disciplinary findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated warnings from the tribunal, continued argumentative behavior after adverse rulings, attempts to contaminate the record, and direct insults to witnesses are aggravating factors. Such conduct may be used to infer motive or pattern (e.g., willingness to submit altered evidence) and to assess fitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of 'open refusal' in excusing noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Open refusal' is recognized as good faith and open noncompliance in order to test an order's validity and can, in narrow circumstances, excuse noncompliance with tribunal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify, noncompliance must be in good faith and openly asserted; mere collateral motions or unsuccessful attempts to vacate/appeal a judgment do not suffice. The practitioner remains obligated to comply pending appeal unless a stay is entered.
